findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Transformation programme Future Sheffield delivering minimal financial benefit in 2025/26; majority of benefits deferred to future years
findings.detail: Future Sheffield is described as 'the Council's primary vehicle for addressing long-term financial sustainability' but 'while early benefits are beginning to emerge, the majority of financial impact is expected in future years.' This means current budget assumptions depend on transformation benefits that have not yet materialised and carry delivery risk.
findings.matters: If the council's medium-term financial strategy depends on transformation programme benefits that are not yet delivering, future budget years could face the same pressures as 2025/26 if the programme slips or underperforms.
findings.figures: No specific benefit figures for 2025/26 disclosed
findings.quote: During 2025/26, work has continued to develop the programme and align it more closely with financial planning. While early benefits are beginning to emerge, the majority of financial impact is expected in future years. Delivery of the programme therefore remains critical to achieving a sustainable financial position over the medium term.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) pressures in high needs continuing outside General Fund but remain material financial risk
findings.detail: DSG pressures, particularly high needs expenditure, sit outside the General Fund position reported here but are flagged as 'a significant financial risk' requiring 'separate statutory accounting arrangements and recovery planning'. This is an additional liabilities layer not captured in the £11.1m headline overspend.
findings.matters: DSG deficits can accumulate as statutory duties that councils cannot avoid. Though accounted separately, high needs spending often spills into General Fund eventually, creating hidden future liabilities.
findings.figures: DSG pressures (amount not disclosed in this report)
findings.quote: The Council continues to manage pressures within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), particularly in relation to high needs expenditure. While these pressures sit outside the General Fund position reported above, they remain a significant financial risk and are subject to separate statutory accounting arrangements and recovery planning.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Housing structural deficit: £2.9m subsidy gap between cost and Housing Benefit recovery
findings.detail: Supported exempt accommodation creates a structural gap between costs incurred and government subsidy recovered. Council describes this as 'a structural financial challenge' and notes it 'has remained consistent throughout the year'. Work to reduce via partnership arrangements and appeals is underway but 'remains a complex area with a degree of uncertainty around the extent and timing of financial benefit.'
findings.matters: This is a structural mismatch between costs and income that cannot be solved by the council alone; it depends on government subsidy rules and the accuracy of provider claims. It is not a discretionary overspend but a policy-driven deficit.
findings.figures: Supported exempt accommodation £2.9m pressure in Housing Benefit
findings.quote: Supported exempt accommodation (£2.9m pressure in Housing Benefit) This pressure sits within Strategic & Enabling Services budgets and reflects the gap between Housing Benefit paid and the amount reimbursed by government for supported accommodation. This pressure has remained consistent throughout the year and continues to represent a structural financial challenge.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Children's placements £9m overspend with unresolved reliance on high-cost external provision
findings.detail: Placements (residential and independent) are £9m over budget with continued demand for complex needs. Recovery actions focus on expanding in-house provision but progress is slow; council states it is 'expanding in-house fostering and residential provision' but placements remain the largest single pressure within Children's Services (£12.1m total overspend).
findings.matters: Children's placements are high-cost per case and volatile; inability to reduce external placements suggests either insufficient in-house capacity or difficulty managing demand, both indicating future cost pressures.
findings.figures: Placements £9.0m overspend; total Children's Services £12.1m overspend; rising demand for residential and independent settings
findings.quote: Placements (£9.0m overspend) – continued demand for care, with more children placed in higher-cost residential and independent settings

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Reserves being drawn down unsustainably to cover structural deficits; £11.1m overspend funded from reserves
findings.detail: Council explicitly states 'This is not a sustainable approach' yet has depleted reserves significantly over recent years and will use them again in 2025/26. Remaining reserves are 'an important part of the Council's financial resilience and must be protected', creating tension with ongoing deficits that require covering.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover revenue overspends indicates the council cannot live within its income. Reserves are one-time sources; exhausting them leaves the council with no buffer for demand shocks or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £11.1m funded from reserves in 2025/26; ongoing reserves depletion; 2024/25 overspend £34.7m, 2023/24 £15.6m
findings.quote: The Council has made significant use of reserves in recent years to manage financial pressures, resulting in a reduction in available balances. The 2025/26 overspend of £11.1m will be funded from reserves, reflecting the continued use of reserves to manage in-year pressures. This is not a sustainable approach.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: £11.1m overspend masked by one-off corporate actions; underlying demand pressures unchanged
findings.detail: The improved headline position (£7.8m better than Q3) came from £13m contingencies release, £9.8m Collection Fund surplus, £3m treasury benefits, and £3.7m vacancy factor savings — none structural. Council acknowledges: 'the improved position is largely due to one-off corporate actions and year-end adjustments, rather than a reduction in demand for services.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether financial improvement is structural or temporary. One-off measures do not solve recurring problems and cannot be relied upon going forward.
findings.figures: £11.1m overspend vs £18.9m Q3 forecast; £13m contingencies; £9.8m Collection Fund surplus; £3m treasury/financing benefits; £3.7m vacancy factor
findings.quote: However, the improved position is largely due to one-off corporate actions and year-end adjustments, rather than a reduction in demand for services. The main drivers of pressure, particularly in social care, SEND and housing, remain in place at year end.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Savings programme delivering only 77% of planned £58.5m target, with £4.5m assessed as permanently undeliverable
findings.detail: Of £13.4m shortfall, £8.9m slipped to next year but £4.5m is undeliverable in-year and requires replacement savings or ongoing budget absorption. Adults' Services particularly weak at 56% delivery. Slippage concentrated in transformation programmes and demand-led services where delivery is proving harder than planned.
findings.matters: A 77% savings delivery rate indicates budget plans rely on actions the council cannot execute reliably. Undeliverable savings must be replaced elsewhere or leave an ongoing structural deficit.
findings.figures: £58.5m planned; £45.1m delivered; £13.4m shortfall; £4.5m undeliverable; Adults 56% delivery vs Neighbourhood Services 98%
findings.quote: The approved 2025/26 budget included £58.5m of savings, of which £45.1m has been delivered in-year, resulting in a shortfall of £13.4m (c.23%). This represents a delivery rate of around 77%, which is lower than in previous years. Of the £13.4m shortfall: around £8.9m relates to slippage into 2026/27, where savings are expected to be delivered later than planned; and around £4.5m is currently assessed as undeliverable in-year, requiring either replacement savings or funding through ongoing budget management.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care £30m overspend driven by uncontrolled demand growth and complex care packages
findings.detail: The largest service pressure (£30m) remains structural: more people requiring support and increasingly complex, expensive care. Some progress on package reviews and stabilisation of costs per case, but overall demand continues rising and planned savings have not delivered in-year, deferring £10.8m (44%) of savings to next year.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically 20-25% of council spending; persistent growth above budget threatens financial sustainability and requires either revenue growth or demand reduction neither of which is assured.
findings.figures: £30.0m overspend; Adults' Services delivered only 56% of planned savings (£10.8m shortfall)
findings.quote: The largest pressure remains within Adults' Social Care. The overspend is mainly due to the cost of care packages, with more people needing support and, increasingly complex and expensive care. Some progress has been made during the year to review and manage packages, and there are early signs that costs per package may be stabilising. However, overall demand continues to rise, and a number of planned savings have not been delivered within the year and are now expected to be delivered next year, meaning the underlying pressure remains.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Complaints handling satisfaction fell to 33.2% (lowest measure) and Stage 1 response time performance is below sector average at 52%
findings.detail: Satisfaction with complaints handling declined year-on-year and is the only perception measure to worsen in 2025/26. Stage 1 responses within timescale are only 52% (target 85%). This is the single worst-performing TSM and a direct outcome of increased demand and capacity pressures. The council acknowledges this is a national trend but remains a regulatory concern.
findings.matters: Poor complaints handling is a regulator priority under the Transparency, Influence and Accountability Standard. Combined with the C3 grade, persistent complaints handling failure could trigger enforcement action. Large repair-related complaint volumes suggest service quality issues are not being resolved quickly.
findings.figures: Satisfaction 33.2% (2025/26, down from 33.8%); Stage 1 responses within timescale 52% (target 85%); Stage 2 responses improved to 22% within timescale (from baseline)
findings.quote: satisfaction with complaints handling remains comparatively low and was the only perception measure that returned a poorer performance in 2025/26 compared to 2024/25, albeit a very small drop from 33.8% to 33.2%. The handling of complaints remains a key area for improvement, both with respect to the speed of response and the way that they are being dealt with.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: New damp and mould reports surged 44% to 2,536 cases in Q4, signalling either worsening stock condition or rising tenant reporting
findings.detail: Pre-Awaab's Law damp and mould cases increased sharply in Q4 (2,536 new cases vs. 1,756 in Q3). While overdue cases fell and the council attributes this to improved reporting and confidence, the volume surge creates service capacity risk. Awaab's Law (September 2023) requires emergency hazards remedied within fixed timeframes; non-compliance exposes tenants to legal claims.
findings.matters: Damp and mould under Awaab's Law carries strict compliance timelines and tenant compensation risk if remediation fails. A 44% case surge suggests either deteriorating stock quality or a backlog of unreported issues now surfacing. Either scenario creates operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 2,536 new damp/mould cases in Q4 2025/26 (vs. 1,756 in Q3); 133 open cases; 92 overdue cases
findings.quote: New reported cases have increased notably, with 2,536 cases raised in Quarter 4 compared to 1,756 in Quarter 3. This reflects improved reporting, stronger internal recording mechanisms, better identification of issues, and increased resident confidence in coming forward. It also reinforces the need to sustain capacity and maintain momentum in case resolution.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Overdue repairs backlog surged to 8,772 in Q4 2025/26, directly degrading tenant satisfaction and operational capacity
findings.detail: Overdue repairs rose significantly in Q4 after sustained improvements. The backlog now totals 8,772 cases (though down from ~23,000 in January 2024). This directly impacted tenant satisfaction with repairs (down 3% in Q4 despite annual improvement). The council has deployed additional managerial and operational resource but this signals ongoing demand-supply imbalance.
findings.matters: Persistent repairs backlog signals service quality risk and operational stress. Tenant satisfaction declining in Q4 despite annual improvement suggests the service is under pressure. Legal disrepair cases (471 open) create liability exposure.
findings.figures: 8,772 overdue repairs at Q4 2025/26; 16,000 repairs in-progress (down from ~36,000 in Jan 2024); 471 open legal disrepair cases; tenant satisfaction with time to repair fell 3% to 72% in Q4
findings.quote: A key contributing factor is the increase in overdue repairs, which rose to 8,772 in Quarter 4. This growing backlog likely impacted tenant experience during this period and constrained the service's ability to complete repairs within target timescales, contributing to the observed decline in satisfaction over the last quarter.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Electrical safety compliance deadline of 1 November 2026 creates operational and regulatory urgency, with 698 properties still non-compliant
findings.detail: All council homes must hold valid Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICR) within a five-year compliance cycle by 1 November 2026. As of Q4, 698 properties (just under 2%) remain non-compliant for over 10 years. The council plans to deliver ~1,000 EICR inspections per month through November 2026 to meet the deadline, but this is a significant acceleration from current throughput.
findings.matters: Failure to meet this statutory deadline could result in regulator action and legal liability. The scale of activity required (1,000 inspections/month) signals capacity risk if contractors cannot deliver.
findings.figures: 698 properties non-compliant as of Q4 2025/26 (down from 758 in Q3); compliance deadline 1 November 2026; target delivery ~1,000 inspections/month
findings.quote: Under revised regulations, all properties must be compliant by 1 November 2026, and the Council is working closely with its two principal contractors to increase delivery capacity accordingly.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: C3 regulatory grade (July 2024) means serious failings the council's current arrangements are not strong enough to fix
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grade in July 2024, the second-worst rating, indicating serious failings in delivering Consumer Standards outcomes. The regulator has not yet deployed enforcement powers but confirmed they will keep this under review. The council is required to develop and deliver a significant change plan.
findings.matters: A C3 grade signals potential for regulator intervention (Performance Improvement Plans, Enforcement Notices, or Management Transfer). This is governance and reputational risk for a borrower, and the regulator specifically stated enforcement powers remain available.
findings.figures: C3 grade (on scale C1–C4, where C1 is compliant and C4 is worst); effective from 9 July 2024
findings.quote: The C3 grade means that there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the Consumer Standards, which the landlord's current arrangements are not strong enough to put right. This will be significantly impacting on service outcomes for tenants and/or accountability to tenants.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Rent arrears increased to £10.1m in Q4, up £350k from Q3, driven by housing management system failures
findings.detail: Current tenant rent arrears rose significantly during Q4 2025/26, with the increase directly attributed to problems with the new housing management system implemented in Q3. Automated processes, system-generated letters, and direct debits all failed, forcing staff onto manual work the team could not sustain. This directly impacts Housing Revenue Account income.
findings.matters: Growing rent arrears reduce the HRA's ability to service debt and fund housing operations. System-driven failures create operational risk and suggest capacity pressures in service delivery.
findings.figures: £10.1m current tenant arrears (Q4 2025/26), up £350k from Q3; £4.34m former tenant arrears
findings.quote: The introduction of the new housing management system in Quarter 3 has impacted rent collection performance. Issues with automated processes, inability to send system generated letters and direct debits not working correctly have all created additional manual work that the team has struggled to maintain.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: EWI2 contractor replaced following unsatisfactory performance; delayed completion to Q3 2026/27
findings.detail: Original contractor on external wall insulation phase 2 underperformed and was replaced. New contractor now tasked with 91 properties, target completion Q3 2026/27. Indicates prior procurement/contract management failure and adds further delay to fire safety remedial programme.
findings.matters: Contractor failure affects schedule, cost control, and programme confidence; replacement adds delay to critical remedial work.
findings.figures: 91 remaining properties; target completion Q3 2026/27
findings.quote: The external wall insulation phase 2 (EWI 2 Airey repair and insulation) has a new contractor appointed following the unsatisfactory performance of the original contractor.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Grant-funded energy efficiency programme underperforming against funding conditions; funder notified of clawback risk
findings.detail: 'Delivery to date is lower than originally profiled' on SHDF3 energy efficiency (grant-funded). 'Funder has been kept informed, as the final grant position may be influenced by overall programme delivery across local authorities.' Risk of grant clawback or reduced future allocations if target expenditure not met.
findings.matters: Grant clawback directly reduces HRA resources; also signals delivery risk that could affect future grant eligibility or borrowing capacity from government schemes.
findings.figures: Specific underspend amount not disclosed; programme is grant-funded with fixed spend conditions
findings.quote: This project is funded by a grant, and in accordance with the conditions of the grant, a certain level of expenditure must be met during year 25/26. Delivery to date is lower than originally profiled, resulting in a variance against budget. The funder has been kept informed, as the final grant position may be influenced by overall programme delivery across local authorities.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Strategic acquisitions for temporary accommodation delayed by structural issues under negotiation with seller
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation acquisitions programme underspent £5.4m (largest single variance) due to 'ongoing negotiations with the seller on structural issues'. Completion pushed from early 2026 to April/May 2026. Suggests due diligence identified defects requiring negotiation on price/remediation.
findings.matters: Structural defects increase lifetime maintenance costs and affect asset quality; negotiations suggest final cost/liability may not yet be settled; impacts HRA long-term asset base.
findings.figures: £5.4m underspend; completion delayed ~3 months
findings.quote: Project delays due to ongoing negotiations with the seller on structural issues delaying completion of acquisition. Acquisition originally due to complete in early 2026 but now delayed until April/May 26

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Building Control sign-off delays stalling external wall insulation remedial programme on fire-risk stock
findings.detail: EWI2 (external wall insulation on Airey properties, which carry known fire risk) has £1.59m underspend due to 'delays in obtaining footings/foundations sign-off from Building Control'. 15 properties scheduled for completion by March 2026 were not completed. Programme now expected to finish Q3 2026/27.
findings.matters: Building Control delays on remedial work to known fire-risk housing expose the council to regulatory and legal risk; suggests process bottlenecks beyond the council's control but affecting safety compliance.
findings.figures: £1.59m underspend; 15 properties delayed; remaining 91 properties targeted for Q3 2026/27
findings.quote: This was due in part to delays in obtaining footings/ foundations sign-off from Building Control, which impacted progress on site.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Tower block fire safety schemes paused due to delays in finalising fire strategies
findings.detail: Fire safety remediation programmes have been 'temporarily paused' because 'delays in finalising Fire Strategies have prevented progression of the design work'. £0.786m underspend on internal fire safety, £0.187m on external bin stores. These are regulatory-critical programmes serving vulnerable residents.
findings.matters: Fire safety is non-negotiable regulatory compliance; pausing critical safety work on high-rise housing suggests systemic governance or regulatory process friction that could impede other compliance obligations.
findings.figures: Tower Blocks Internal Fire Safety Works £0.786m variance; External Bin Stores £0.187m variance
findings.quote: Tower Block Internals and Fire Risk Assessment External schemes have been temporarily paused – Delays in finalising Fire Strategies have prevented progression of the design work.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Housing capital programme delivered only 82% of budget, continuing pattern of significant underspend
findings.detail: Final outturn for 2025/26 was £66.5m against £80.7m approved budget, a £14.2m underspend (17.6%). This repeats 2024/25 (£25.4m of £28.7m, 11.5% underspend) and follows prior years with 14-15% typical slippage. The persistent pattern suggests systematic delivery issues rather than one-off delays.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence in councils' capital delivery capability; serial slippage of this scale indicates execution risk and raises questions about budget planning accuracy.
findings.figures: £66.5m actual vs £80.7m budget; £14.2m underspend; comparison: 2024/25 underspend £14.3m on smaller budget
findings.quote: The Final Housing Capital Programme out-turn position at the end of March 2026 was £66.5m. This was (£14.2m) under the approved programme budget of £80.7m.

findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - Finance & Performance Committee
findings.headline: Children's placements overspent by £9m and remain driven by high-cost residential settings with no clear demand containment
findings.detail: Children's Services total overspend of £12.1m, with £9m from placements in residential and independent settings. The paper describes 'continued demand for care' and notes improvements are 'mainly due to one-off factors and timing differences rather than a reduction in underlying demand.'
findings.matters: Like ASC, placements are a demand-led cost with escalating complexity and costs. The council describes recovery actions around expanding in-house provision and improving commissioning, but these show limited progress and rely on external factors.
findings.figures: £9m placements overspend; £12.1m total children's services overspend; 85% delivery rate on children's savings (£2.3m shortfall)
findings.quote: Placements (£9.0m overspend) – continued demand for care, with more children placed in higher-cost residential and independent settings

findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - Finance & Performance Committee
findings.headline: Council implemented tight recruitment restrictions and spend controls contributing £4.8m to balance, flagged as 'difficult but necessary' and continuing into 2026/27
findings.detail: Recruitment freeze and discretionary spend controls contributed £3.7m salary savings and £1.1m discretionary reductions. The paper notes these 'have been difficult but necessary and will remain in place into 2026/27,' indicating the council had to restrict basic operational capacity to hit financial targets.
findings.matters: Operational restrictions are a sign of financial stress. Freezing recruitment impairs service capacity and workforce development. Using these as a recurring financial management tool suggests the underlying business model is unbalanced.
findings.figures: £4.8m total contribution from controls; £3.7m salary/agency; £1.1m discretionary spend reductions
findings.quote: Essential to achieving this improved position has been the continued use of spend controls and tighter recruitment restrictions. These measures have made a measurable contribution to the in-year financial position by around £4.8m

findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - Finance & Performance Committee
findings.headline: The £11.1m overspend is being funded from reserves, continuing a pattern the council acknowledges is 'not a sustainable approach'
findings.detail: The paper states reserves 'have been subject to significant use in recent years to manage financial pressures, resulting in a reduction in available balances.' The 2025/26 overspend requires drawing £11.1m from reserves to balance the budget. The council explicitly labels this 'not a sustainable approach' yet acknowledges reserves remain essential.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurring operational deficits rather than unexpected events indicates financial deterioration. Reserves are the council's buffer against shocks; depleting them for routine overspends suggests the council is approaching the limit of its financial resilience.
findings.figures: £11.1m reserve drawdown for 2025/26 overspend; reserves reduced over recent years; ongoing reliance on reserves to mask deficits
findings.quote: The 2025/26 overspend of £11.1m will be funded from reserves, reflecting the continued use of reserves to manage in-year pressures. This is not a sustainable approach.

findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - Finance & Performance Committee
findings.headline: The council failed to deliver 23% of planned £58.5m savings programme, with only 77% delivery rate
findings.detail: £45.1m of £58.5m planned savings delivered, leaving £13.4m shortfall. Of this, £8.9m slipped to 2026/27 but £4.5m is classified as undeliverable and requires replacement savings. Adult services only achieved 56% delivery rate on planned savings.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings signals weakness in financial control and execution. If medium-term financial plans include undeliverable savings, the council's future budget forecasts are unreliable. This pattern was lower than prior years.
findings.figures: £13.4m shortfall out of £58.5m planned (23%); 77% delivery rate; Adults' Services 56% delivery rate (£10.8m undelivered)
findings.quote: The approved 2025/26 budget included £58.5m of savings, of which £45.1m has been delivered in-year, resulting in a shortfall of £13.4m (c.23%). This represents a delivery rate of around 77%, which is lower than in previous years.

findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - Finance & Performance Committee
findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £30m with rising demand uncontained despite cost review efforts
findings.detail: ASC is the single largest service pressure. The paper describes efforts to review and manage care packages, but states explicitly that 'overall demand has continued to rise' and planned savings 'have not been delivered within the year.' Rising complexity of care packages continues to exceed budget assumptions.
findings.matters: ASC is the largest discretionary spend for councils. A £30m uncontained overspend on demand-led services shows the council has lost financial control over its single largest cost driver, with no indication this will improve.
findings.figures: £30m adult social care overspend; delivery of ASC planned savings only 56% (£10.8m shortfall)
findings.quote: The largest pressure remains within Adults' Social Care. The overspend is mainly due to the cost of care packages, with more people needing support and, increasingly complex and expensive care.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q4 Capital Programme Final Outturn
findings.headline: Heart of the City II prudential borrowing scheme dependent on future capital receipts and lettings income to offset debt costs
findings.detail: Heart of the City II scheme is funded with £1.85m prudential borrowing and is 'now largely complete with all blocks now operative with just minor lettings allowance now remaining.' The council states 'Future revenues and capital receipts from developed sites are expected to offset future principal and revenue costs' and notes it 'keeps this under ongoing review.' This creates revenue risk: if lettings or capital receipts fail to materialise or fall short of assumptions, the council faces unbudgeted revenue costs.
findings.matters: Prudential borrowing creates ongoing revenue costs that must be offset by asset sales or lettings income; if market conditions weaken or lettings underperform relative to assumptions, the council faces unanticipated revenue pressures; ongoing review language suggests some uncertainty about outcomes.
findings.figures: £1.85m prudential borrowing; debt service costs must be offset by 'future revenues and capital receipts'; scheme now complete except minor lettings; represents 1% of capital budget but creates multi-year revenue obligation
findings.quote: Future revenues and capital receipts from developed sites are expected to offset future principal and revenue costs. We keep this under ongoing review.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q4 Capital Programme Final Outturn
findings.headline: Construction market cost escalation and supply chain fragility creating ongoing pressure on capital programme affordability and deliverability
findings.detail: The council reports 'Cost escalation and volatility within live projects and new tenders continue to put pressure on approved budgets,' with labour costs remaining the primary driver. Supply chain challenges include 'Contractors and suppliers remain risk-averse, competition is reduced in some areas, and skills shortages continue to affect programme certainty.' Multiple schemes overspent: Newstead General Needs (+£1.43m) due to utilities diversion and design changes; Stocksbridge Community Hub (+£0.6m) due to discovery of contaminated materials. Council response includes 'active rephasing, value engineering and stronger commercial management'; forward conditions expected to remain challenging.
findings.matters: Cost escalation reduces programme affordability and forces value engineering or scope reduction; fragile supply chains and contractor risk-aversion directly affect programme deliverability and timeline certainty; structural market pressures are expected to continue, making future cost forecasting uncertain.
findings.figures: £1.43m Newstead overspend; £0.6m Stocksbridge overspend; 'Tender returns continue to outpace budgets'; multiple schemes requiring value engineering and rephasing
findings.quote: Cost escalation, labour shortages, supply chain fragility and cautious contractor behaviour have required active rephasing, value engineering and stronger commercial management across the programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q4 Capital Programme Final Outturn
findings.headline: Transforming Cities Fund schemes face approval delays and extended slippage, creating cash flow and external funding clawback risk
findings.detail: TCF Nether Edge Wedge scheme (£1.09m overspend) remains pending SYMCA formal approval at year-end despite funds being allocated. TCF Magna-Meadowhall Cycling (£1.1m slippage) now expected to complete November 2026 due to Work Package A delays and lack of contractor financial information. Multiple other TCF schemes delayed. The council explicitly warns that 'Time-limited external funding remains at risk where programmes slip.'
findings.matters: Time-limited external funding carries clawback risk if delivery slips; approval delays create cash flow timing uncertainty and affect borrowing forecasts; programme delays could trigger funding withdrawal or conditions changes from external bodies.
findings.figures: £13m TCF funding in 2025-26; TCF, Levelling Up Fund, and Homes England funding represent £31.4m (24% of capital programme); multiple schemes delayed beyond March 2026
findings.quote: Funds are allocated from SYMCA to meet this awaiting formal approvals

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q4 Capital Programme Final Outturn
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant statutory service faces backlog due to delivery partner performance issues
findings.detail: The £4.8m Disabled Facilities Grant programme slipped £1.1m (23%) due to 'performance challenges associated with the Council's delivery partner.' Demand for adaptations 'remains significant' and all schemes are 'fully committed,' but completion was delayed and backlog recovery depends on contractor performance stabilising. This affects a statutory service for vulnerable residents.
findings.matters: DFG is a statutory service; delivery partner failure creates service quality and potential legal/reputational risk; uncertain backlog recovery is contingent on third-party performance outside council direct control.
findings.figures: £1.1m slippage on £4.8m budget; completion affected by backlog; backlog recovery measures being implemented but contingent on contractor performance
findings.quote: Demand for disabled adaptations remains significant, with high levels of approved and committed work continued throughout 2025/26; however, completion of works was affected by a backlog and performance challenges associated with the Council's delivery partner.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q4 Capital Programme Final Outturn
findings.headline: Housing acquisition and major works programmes face substantial delivery delays affecting capital investment strategy
findings.detail: Multiple housing schemes are significantly delayed: Strategic Temporary Accommodation (£5.4m slippage) is held up by structural issues in negotiations; Local Authority Housing Fund Phase 3 (£2.1m slippage) has four property purchases and refurbishments deferred to 2026-27; Passive Fire Safety (£1.96m slippage) experienced slow contractor onboarding; External Wall Insulation Phase 2 (£1.59m slippage) missed March completion waiting for Building Control sign-off; Manor/Pennine Housing (£0.92m slippage) delayed five plots until mid-April with defect work extending to 2028-29. These delays reflect structural and market constraints affecting housing delivery.
findings.matters: Housing drives council revenue and service delivery; acquisition delays reduce housing supply and defer income; slippage extending into 2026-27 and 2027-28 signals market or strategic execution issues affecting medium-term capital planning.
findings.figures: £12m+ in housing slippage across major programmes; housing represents 48% of total capital budget (£80.8m approved); Strategic Temp Accommodation acquisition delayed from early 2026 to April/May 26
findings.quote: Project delays due to ongoing negotiations with the seller on structural issues delaying completion of acquisition. Acquisition originally due to complete in early 2026 but now delayed until April/May 26.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: Audit fees increased £112k above scale plus £52k build-back assurance work pending approval
findings.detail: Total audit fees rose to £602.4k from base of £490.2k. Variations driven by transaction listing complexity (requiring extended samples), asset classification issues, valuation challenges, housing data gaps, and new standards (IFRS16, ISA600 revised). Further build-back assurance fees of £52.9k subject to PSAA approval.
findings.matters: Significant audit fee increases indicate control weaknesses requiring deep auditor investigation. This signals elevated audit risk and future compliance costs.
findings.figures: Base fee £490.2k; approved variations £55.8k; pending approval £59.3k + £52.9k build-back; total £602.4k
findings.quote: Fee Variations approved by PSAA - £55,809; Fee variations agreed with management but subject to PSAA approval £59,277

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: No formal control to ensure timely removal of employee leavers from payroll systems
findings.detail: Auditors identified absence of formal control confirming employee leavers are promptly removed from systems. Payroll claims to process immediately upon notification, but there is no control ensuring managers submit notifications timely. Only informal reactive checks exist during monthly processing.
findings.matters: Absence of formal leaver controls creates risk of inappropriate payments, overpayments, and inaccurate workforce data—a basic financial control failure.
findings.figures: No formal control documented
findings.quote: During the walkthrough of the employee leavers process it was identified that there is not a control in place that confirms that leavers are appropriately removed from systems in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: Right to Buy disposals of £13m in year while council dwelling valuations increased £124m due to market prices
findings.detail: The council disposed of £13m of Right to Buy assets while valuations of remaining council dwellings (£1,747m total) increased £124m in response to Sheffield housing market price increases. This indicates significant exposure to property market conditions.
findings.matters: Council dwelling valuations are volatile and cyclical; large year-on-year movements indicate balance sheet exposure to property market downturns.
findings.figures: Right to Buy disposals £13m; dwelling valuation increase £124m; total stock £1,747m
findings.quote: The Council have disposed of £13m right to buy assets, and the valuation has increased by £124m in line with an increase in prices within the Housing Market in Sheffield.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: LGPS pension asset of £53.3m now recognized alongside unfunded scheme liability of £45.2m
findings.detail: The council has an unusually large Local Government Pension Scheme net asset of £53.3m as at 31 March 2025, with £445m actuarial gain primarily from discount rate increase from 4.8% to 5.8%. Auditors note pension surpluses are growing across the sector but involve complex accounting treatment.
findings.matters: Large pension assets are volatile and market-sensitive. Auditors noting complex recognition requirements signals downside risk if actuarial assumptions reverse.
findings.figures: LGPS net Pension Asset £53.3m; unfunded scheme liability £45.2m; actuarial gain £445.4m
findings.quote: The Council have a LGPS net Pension Asset of £53.3m and a Pension Liability for unfunded scheme of £(45.2m) as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: £98-149m of assets incorrectly classified as surplus subsequently reclassified to operational
findings.detail: Material volumes of assets were initially classified as surplus assets in draft accounts but did not meet CIPFA definition. These had to be reclassified to operational or other land and buildings after management review. Indicates weak asset classification controls.
findings.matters: Asset classification errors of this magnitude indicate poor asset management processes and potential risk of undisclosed disposals or value impairment.
findings.figures: £98-149m of assets reclassified from Surplus Assets
findings.quote: A material movement between Surplus assets and Other Land and Buildings was made to the final financial statements to reflect the appropriate treatment.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: Non-pay expenditure population contained £1.3bn debits and £1.1bn credits of reversing entries not part of actual balance
findings.detail: Transaction listing populations for audit testing included massive volumes of reversing entries that artificially inflated gross transaction values. This required extended sample testing and indicates weak transaction reporting capability and poor segregation of reversing vs. operational entries.
findings.matters: Inability to cleanly report transactions indicates weak financial systems and control environment, affecting reliability of spend data and management's ability to monitor expenditure.
findings.figures: Non-pay expenditure: £1.3bn debit and £1.1bn credit reversing entries
findings.quote: Populations presented for sample testing included significant levels of transactions that inflated the Gross levels of Debits and Credits, for example non-pay expenditure included £1.3bn of Debit and £1.1bn of Credit balances.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: One significant value for money weakness identified in Adult Care and Wellbeing budget setting
findings.detail: Auditors identified one significant weakness in arrangements for securing value for money, specifically in Adult Care and Wellbeing budget setting and pressures. This is under the Financial Sustainability domain and indicates inadequate management of the council's largest and most volatile budget.
findings.matters: Adult social care weakness indicates risk of service failure or unexpected financial pressure in the budget that typically absorbs 40%+ of council spending.
findings.figures: One significant weakness under Financial Sustainability domain
findings.quote: We have identified one significant weakness under the Financial sustainability Domain linked to Adult Care and Wellbeing budget setting and pressures.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: £121.1m major sporting facilities returned from Sheffield City Trust in settlement of capital debtor
findings.detail: Three major sporting facilities were returned to the council by Sheffield City Trust in lieu of cash repayment of a capital debtor. This involved significant accounting entries and a grossing-up misstatement auditors had to correct, indicating previous capital commitment complexity.
findings.matters: A £121m asset transfer signals substantial prior commitments and raises questions about original transaction structure and why it required asset rather than cash settlement.
findings.figures: £121.1m valuation of Major Sporting Facilities; £115.1m grossing-up adjustment required
findings.quote: We have tested the capital financing entries that are required to account for the derecognition of the Sheffield City Trust debtor and recognition of the three Major Sporting Facilities that were handed back to the Council

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: £39.6m equal pay provision recognized in 2024-25, funded from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: A material provision was recognized when the quantum of backdated equal pay claims could finally be valued. This was a previously unquantified liability now crystallized and funded from earmarked reserves, reducing available resources.
findings.matters: A large liability suddenly becoming quantifiable in year indicates financial management weakness and materially depletes reserves available for other purposes.
findings.figures: £39.6m provision recognized; funded from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Being the Equal Pay provision recognised in the 24-25 financial statements when the quantum of the backdated claims were able to be reasonably valued. The value of the claims being paid for by the use of earmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: SCC ISA 260 -2024-25 - Audit and Standards Committee 19.3.2026
findings.headline: Council issued modified audit opinion after removing prior disclaimer but still modified for opening balance uncertainties
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24, but auditors have removed that for 2024-25 after building sufficient evidence. The opinion remains modified due to disclaimed opening balances. This represents partial resolution of a 2-year audit backlog but signals ongoing financial statement uncertainty.
findings.matters: Modified opinions indicate financial statement uncertainty material enough to require auditor qualification. Lenders and finance directors need to understand the scope of that uncertainty.
findings.figures: Disclaimers for 2022/23 and 2023/24; modified opinion for 2024/25
findings.quote: We will be able to remove the disclaimed opinion that was issued in the two prior periods, and we will be giving a modified opinion for 2024-25 due to the impact of disclaimed balances in the opening balance sheet.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Construction inflation at 4% driving project delays and budget overruns
findings.detail: Construction inflation is 'currently running at around 4%' and is 'baked into all our lives', driving tender prices that exceed budgets estimated years ago. This is causing delays to capital schemes when actual costs exceed budgeted amounts.
findings.matters: A council facing revenue pressure and tight funding margins will struggle to absorb inflation-driven cost overruns. This creates project delivery risk and potential for scope cuts or delays that reduce service outcomes.
findings.figures: Construction inflation approximately 4%
findings.quote: Construction inflation is currently running at around 4%; whilst this is lower than the recent peaks, the increase in prices is now baked into all our lives, driving up prices and causing delays to capital schemes when tender prices exceed budgets that were estimated some years ago.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Academy conversion policy reduces central government formula funding while retaining council maintenance obligations on some schools
findings.detail: Central government policy mandates all new schools become academies, which transfers maintenance responsibility away from the council's Local Education Authority role. However, formula funding (which is driven by pupil numbers) follows pupils to academies, reducing the council's education budget while the council retains responsibility for ensuring sufficient school places.
findings.matters: This creates a structural squeeze: the council loses revenue funding but retains statutory obligations to ensure school places exist, potentially forcing capital investment to solve a revenue problem.
findings.figures: Education capital budget £13.2m over five years (1.9% of total)
findings.quote: It will also subsequently reduce central grant funding (which is formula-driven based on pupil numbers), with the risk that this will leave the Council with the significant investment requirements with even more limited funds to undertake this with.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Corporate estate has significant unfunded backlog maintenance; needs 'radical approach'
findings.detail: The council manages 807 establishments and 873 buildings (excluding housing and schools) and acknowledges it has 'significant backlog maintenance' requiring 'a radical approach to ensure our corporate estate is sustainable in the medium to long term'. No specific funding allocation is identified for this liability.
findings.matters: Backlog maintenance on a large corporate estate represents an unquantified future liability. The language ('radical approach', 'sustainability in medium term') suggests the council recognizes this cannot be funded through normal means—raising the risk of service disruption, asset deterioration, or emergency spending.
findings.figures: 807 establishments and 873 buildings requiring maintenance; no capital budget allocated to Adult Health & Social Care or Economic Development in years after 2026-27
findings.quote: We have significant backlog maintenance, and we will need a radical approach to ensure our corporate estate is sustainable in the medium to long term.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Heart of the City II exit strategy under review in January 2026, original asset-sale assumption may not hold
findings.detail: The council borrowed approximately £20m+ on prudential borrowing to fund Heart of the City II development, with an original assumption that blocks would be sold once let. Officers are now reviewing this strategy 'to leverage the financial advantages of holding the blocks for longer' rather than selling. A new exit strategy goes to Finance Committee in January 2026. This represents material uncertainty on a major borrowing decision.
findings.matters: A significant prudential borrowing commitment was premised on asset sale proceeds reducing debt and generating capital receipts. If this strategy changes to holding assets longer (or permanently), the debt repayment profile changes and revenue budget pressure increases indefinitely.
findings.figures: £20m external grant funding secured; Heart of the City II prudential borrowing reduced from £0.422m (2025-26) to £0.065m (2026-27)
findings.quote: The original exit strategy assumed that most of the Blocks would be sold once completed and fully let. Officers are currently reviewing the efficacy of this strategy to leverage the financial advantages of holding the blocks for longer.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: External funding is described as critical and increasingly uncertain, concentrated through SYMCA
findings.detail: The council states external funding is 'critical to our ability to invest in our city', yet government grant funding in the capital programme drops from £35m in 2026-27 to £0 by 2029-30. The council is increasingly channelling project-specific grants through the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority, creating a single point of dependency.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on funding sustainability. When the largest part of your spending plan (£340.9m of £685.4m) depends on grants that are shrinking to zero, and strategic control is shifting to a combined authority, there is material execution risk.
findings.quote: Continuing to secure external funding is critical to our ability to invest in our city.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account under pressure from rent cap policy and Right to Buy acceleration, with £3.4m strategic decision point for 2026-27
findings.detail: The council faces a £3.4m funding cliff depending on whether it implements new rent convergence policy (national formula rents). If not implemented, this money must be cut from housing capital contribution. Meanwhile, a 'flood of Right to Buy applications in advance of the deadline' is accelerating stock loss and reducing the rental income base. Housing is 80.5% of the five-year capital programme.
findings.matters: Housing capital is the largest part of the programme and HRA is the largest funding source. Policy changes reducing rental income (Right to Buy) and creating binary funding decisions (rent convergence) create unpredictability in the council's largest investment area.
findings.figures: Housing capital programme £551.9m of £685.4m total (5-year); HRA contribution £340.9m of £685.4m total funding (49.7%); rent convergence policy worth up to £3.4m in 2026-27
findings.quote: And whilst the Right to Buy has been curtailed, the changes announced this year have seen a flood of Right to Buy applications in advance of the deadline.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Investment Pipeline 2026-2057
findings.headline: Revenue budget crisis directly constrains capital spending capacity
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is in an 'extremely challenging financial position, particularly on the revenue budget' which 'impacts on our capital spending'. The corporate investment fund is described as 'a finite pot of money and calls on these funds vastly exceed the sum available'. This matters because prudential borrowing repayments must come from revenue budgets that are themselves under pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that capital programme delivery depends on revenue budget stability, which this council describes as extremely constrained. Revenue sustainability directly affects debt repayment capacity.
findings.figures: 5-year capital programme £685.4m; £162.2m (23.7%) funded by prudential borrowing; housing accounts for £551.9m of five-year total
findings.quote: The Council is currently in an extremely challenging financial position, particularly on the revenue budget. This impacts on our capital spending.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Majority of medium-term financial stability dependent on Future Sheffield transformation programme delivering £10.4m in 2026/27 plus further savings in later years
findings.detail: The budget strategy is heavily concentrated on the Future Sheffield transformation programme. The council states it is 'expected to deliver the majority of the savings needed to place the Council on a stable footing' with £10.4m of savings confirmed for 2026/27 and 'further significant benefits planned in subsequent years'. Without these savings materialising, the council would lack the financial capacity to balance future budgets.
findings.matters: Creates concentration of risk on a single major programme; any significant slippage or underdelivery would force the council to revisit already-tight savings or drawdown constrained reserves
findings.figures: £10.4m savings from Future Sheffield in 2026/27; 'majority' of medium-term savings dependent on programme
findings.quote: Recent reports confirm that Future Sheffield is expected to deliver the majority of the medium-term savings needed to stabilise the Council's financial position, with £10.4m of savings already confirmed for 2026/27 and further significant benefits planned in subsequent years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: DSG statutory override ends 1 April 2028; councils will fund 10% of DSG deficits with full impact not yet quantified
findings.detail: The government is ending the statutory override that currently shields councils from DSG deficits. From 2028 onwards, government will fund 90% and councils must fund 10%. Sheffield reports it is 'not in the position where removal of the statutory override would immediately place the council at risk of issuing a Section 114 notice' but says 'the risk to the council would increase' and is 'awaiting further detail' from government on full implications.
findings.matters: Creates quantified future unfunded liability once statutory protection ends; full impact not yet known and risk is not zero even for Sheffield
findings.figures: 10% of DSG deficits to be funded by council from 1 April 2028; exact exposure to be confirmed by government
findings.quote: The Final Local Government Finance Settlement published in February 2026 confirmed the Government's approach to ending the statutory override from 1 April 2028. 90% of the deficit will be funded with the council required to fund the remaining 10%. Further detail will be published by Government in the coming weeks.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Strategic Role Review Programme for equal pay claims requires £8.0m, up £3.3m year-on-year with no end date stated
findings.detail: The council is in a Strategic Role Review Programme reviewing all workforce roles for equal pay compliance. £8.0m of temporary funding has been set aside to settle historic equal pay claims and cover job evaluation costs. This represents a £3.3m increase from the prior year, funded from earmarked reserves. The document does not indicate when settlements will conclude.
findings.matters: Material and growing equal pay liability suggests prior governance/compliance issues; ongoing trajectory and ultimate cost remain unclear, creating budget exposure
findings.figures: £8.0m set aside; £3.3m increase from prior year
findings.quote: In 2024, The Council embarked on a Strategic Role Review Programme in response to equal pay claims. The programme is reviewing all roles across the Council's workforce to ensure all staff are paid equally. £8.0m of temporary funding has been set aside towards the financial liability of settling historic claims

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Unearmarked reserves at £16.9m benchmark low compared to peer major cities, limiting financial resilience
findings.detail: The council's unearmarked reserves—the buffer for unexpected costs or savings shortfalls—stand at £16.9m. The document explicitly flags this as a weakness: 'unearmarked reserves set aside to deal with unknown emergencies, at £16.9m, benchmarks low compared to other authorities.' This leaves minimal headroom for absorbing pressures.
findings.matters: Constrained unearmarked reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb service demand shocks or savings delivery failures without breaching statutory balance requirements
findings.figures: Unearmarked reserves £16.9m; noted as benchmarking low vs. other major cities
findings.quote: Unearmarked reserves set aside to deal with unknown emergencies, at £16.9m, benchmarks low compared to other authorities.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £23.3m savings required for 2026/27 balance with S151 warning some will not deliver in full or on time
findings.detail: The council has proposed £23.3m of savings to balance the 2026/27 budget. However the S151 Officer acknowledges delivery risk: 'there is a risk that a proportion may not have a full-year impact in 2026/27' and 'it is inevitable there will be unforeseen difficulties in implementing some schemes, or these schemes will not deliver the full amounts expected.' Only £13.2m of contingency has been set aside to absorb shortfalls, leaving a gap.
findings.matters: If savings slippage exceeds the £13.2m contingency, the council will need to draw on constrained reserves to balance the year, with no clear plan B
findings.figures: £23.3m savings required; £13.2m contingency set aside
findings.quote: In practice some of these schemes might prove difficult to implement in whole or part following consultation.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £18.9m overspend in 2025/26 draining reserves, with S151 officer warning council cannot sustain further draws
findings.detail: Despite strong in-year management to reduce an earlier Q1 overspend, the council expects a £18.9m overspend in 2025/26. The S151 officer explicitly states the Council's financial position deteriorated due to funds needed to support this overspend, and warns that reserves cannot indefinitely mitigate further overspends: 'The Council cannot continue mitigating overspends from reserves indefinitely, or it will become financially unsustainable.'
findings.matters: Eroding reserves are the council's only buffer for delivery risk; further overspends would force into stressed decisions and potentially unsustainable reserve depletion
findings.figures: £18.9m overspend in 2025/26; year-end position expected 'under £20m'
findings.quote: The Council's financial position has deteriorated during 2025/26 due to funds required to support the in-year overspend of £18.9m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Stock Increase Programme at risk of delivering homes costing more than market value without external funding
findings.detail: Council aims to increase stock by 839 homes (2025/26-2028/29) as part of a 1,000-home target. However, it states "The current economic conditions mean there is a risk that homes delivered directly by the Council will cost the HRA more than their resultant market value, due to high construction costs and high site abnormal costs, unless additional external funding can be secured." Council notes this is "a similar issue faced by many providers."
findings.matters: Delivering housing at below market cost drains reserves and affects financial viability. The program is key to government housing policy and the council's strategic ambitions, so viability risk threatens both program and finances.
findings.figures: 839 homes 2025/26-2028/29; 1,000 homes target to 2028/29; £89.4m allocated to Stock Increase 2026/27
findings.quote: The current economic conditions mean there is a risk that homes delivered directly by the Council will cost the HRA more than their resultant market value, due to high construction costs and high site abnormal costs, unless additional external funding can be secured.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Additional borrowing required from 2028/29 as capital reserves run down
findings.detail: Over the 5-year business plan, capital reserves are used to fund investment in earlier years. Borrowing is expected to remain "fairly steady" through 2028/29, but council states "It is anticipated additional borrowing would be required from 2028/29." This signals medium-term financing need and suggests current reserve depletion strategy has a defined endpoint.
findings.matters: Additional borrowing increases annual debt service costs and reduces financial flexibility. The timing suggests capital spending plan may need revision or revenue contributions increased to avoid borrowing.
findings.figures: Additional borrowing anticipated from 2028/29 onwards; current interest on borrowing £12.1m (2026/27)
findings.quote: It is anticipated additional borrowing would be required from 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Repairs budget rising 8% to £68.5m with stock condition data still incomplete
findings.detail: Repairs budget increased from £63.4m (2024/25 outturn) to £68.5m (2026/27 forecast). Council is "setting a repairs service budget that more accurately reflects current and projected demand." However, stock surveys are only 57% complete, meaning council is still discovering full backlog scope. Awaab's Law (damp/mould compliance) enforcement tightened October 2025 with extended hazard coverage 2026-2027, driving additional repair demand.
findings.matters: Rising repairs costs compress resources available for capital investment in compliance and improvements. Incomplete stock survey data means council is likely still discovering backlog, so further budget increases may be required in future years.
findings.figures: Repairs £68.5m 2026/27 vs £63.4m 2024/25 outturn (+8%); 57% stock surveyed
findings.quote: we are setting a repairs service budget that more accurately reflects current and projected demand.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Multiple overlapping regulatory mandates creating "significant financial pressures" with no government funding committed
findings.detail: Council faces Building Safety Act compliance (ongoing investment required), Awaab's Law damp and mould enforcement (tightening requirements 2026-2027), Decent Homes Standard updates (pending, council states these "will create significant financial pressures"), and EPC C by 2030. None of the policy sections show government committing funding for these mandates. Council is "preparing" and "reviewing" impact but cannot yet cost the full requirements.
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory mandates force difficult trade-offs between compliance, maintenance, and affordability. Multiple simultaneous requirements with uncertain costs and timelines create planning risk and potentially constrain capital investment in other areas.
findings.figures: Building Safety affects 7+ storey properties; Awaab's Law enforcement extended through 2027; Decent Homes updates pending; EPC C deadline 2030
findings.quote: these changes will create significant financial pressures on the HRA to ensure all housing stock meets the updated requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Revenue reserve of £15.8m is significantly inadequate against identified financial risks
findings.detail: The council's unearmarked revenue reserve is £15.8m. The council explicitly states that "The financial impact of the above risks far exceeds the reserve held." While the council argues the likelihood of all risks occurring in one year is low, it acknowledges major reserve shortfall relative to identified risks including regulatory compliance, rising repairs costs, health and safety failures, and increased borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against adverse events. Inadequate reserves mean the HRA has limited ability to absorb shocks such as a spike in emergency repairs, higher rent arrears, further stock losses, or unexpected regulatory costs.
findings.figures: £15.8m reserve; identified risks "far exceed" this amount
findings.quote: The financial impact of the above risks far exceeds the reserve held.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: 920 Right to Buy sales expected by March 2027 with 4,280 total stock losses over 30 years
findings.detail: A surge in Right to Buy applications before a November 2024 deadline means 920 homes are assumed sold by March 2027, with the council expecting to lose 4,280 homes over the 30-year plan (at 120 per year thereafter). The council explicitly states "This is a significant reduction in social homes for the city which already has an affordable housing shortfall." Council stock will decline from 38,040 homes now to 35,379 by 2055.
findings.matters: Each Right to Buy sale reduces rental income, increases relative fixed costs per home, and shrinks the asset base. The concentration of 920 sales through March 2027 accelerates near-term impact on the business plan.
findings.figures: 920 RTB sales to March 2027; 4,280 over 30 years; stock declining from 38,040 to 35,379
findings.quote: 920 of these are assumed to have been completed by March 2027 as the impact of the changes to legislation around Right to Buy sales led to a sharp increase in applications before the deadline in November 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: New SAP 10 energy rating methodology from June 2026 could dramatically worsen the EPC C challenge by 2030
findings.detail: SAP 10 is introduced in June 2026 as the new methodology for calculating energy performance and is "more comprehensive than previous versions." Council notes that "early indications suggest that SAP 10 may result in a greater number of homes being rated in EPC Band D or below, which could significantly increase the scale of the challenge in achieving EPC Band C targets by 2030." Council is "currently assessing its full impact" but cannot yet quantify how many additional properties will need upgrade.
findings.matters: Government mandates EPC C for all socially rented homes by 2030. The SAP 10 impact could substantially increase required capital investment beyond current planning assumptions, creating an unquantified but potentially significant unfunded liability.
findings.figures: SAP 10 introduced June 2026; government target EPC C by 2030; £13.9m allocated for SAP C and Energy Efficiency over 5 years (budget may be insufficient)
findings.quote: Early indications suggest that SAP 10 may result in a greater number of homes being rated in EPC Band D or below, which could significantly increase the scale of the challenge in achieving EPC Band C targets by 2030.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - HRA Business Plan 2026-27 Appendix Report - Updated Section 9
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing inspection likely from 2026 with only 57% of stock fully surveyed
findings.detail: The council has not yet been inspected under the new RSH consumer regulation regime, but inspection is "highly likely" from 2026 onwards on a four-year cycle. However, only 57% of council assets had completed full stock condition surveys by October 2025. Other councils' inspections have identified common issues including "gaps in stock condition data, health and safety compliance failures (e.g., overdue gas and fire checks), large repair backlogs, and weaknesses in tenant engagement and complaints handling."
findings.matters: RSH inspections result in grading C1-C4 with C1 (3 councils) meeting standards and C4 (2 councils) indicating very serious failings. Poor gradings affect regulatory standing, financing, and tenant confidence. Incomplete stock survey data suggests council may not be fully prepared.
findings.figures: 57% stock surveyed as of October 2025; 35 councils inspected nationally with 3 C1, 14 C2, 22 C3, 2 C4 gradings
findings.quote: At the end of October 2025, 57% of all assets have received full stock condition surveys.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: HRA Responsive Repairs overspend of £4.8m driven by £6.5m subcontractor and agency costs plus material inflation
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account Responsive Repairs are overrunning by £4.8m, with £6.5m in subcontractor and agency costs and £1.3m in transport and material increases. The council attributes this to cost inflation, new legislation (damp & mould compliance), and increased demand.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on agency and subcontractor labour suggests insufficient internal workforce capacity. New compliance requirements (damp & mould) create ongoing structural cost pressures on the HRA.
findings.figures: £4.8m overspend; £6.5m subcontractor/agency costs; £1.3m material cost increases
findings.quote: £4.8m overspend driven by: £6.5m in subcontractor and agency costs; £1.3m increase in transport & material costs; Cost inflation, additional legislation (e.g. damp & mould) and increased demand

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: SEND transport overspend of £6.6m with £3.1m savings shortfall due to implementation delays and coordination dependencies
findings.detail: Transport costs are overrunning by £6.6m due to rising pupil numbers, complex timetables, and fleet capacity limits. Children's Services savings shortfalls of £3.1m include SEND transport demand management initiatives (Travel Trainers, Personal Travel Budgets) that require coordination with SYMCA and SENDSARS, subject to consultation and academic year timing.
findings.matters: SEND transport represents structural cost pressure across councils. Delays in implementing demand-management schemes indicate implementation challenges and dependency on external partners, limiting the council's ability to control costs.
findings.figures: £6.6m transport overspend; £3.1m Children's Services savings shortfalls
findings.quote: £6.6m transport overspend due to rising pupil numbers, complex timetables, and fleet capacity limits

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: Children & Families Placements overrunning by £8.8m including £1m unachieved 2024-25 savings linked to failed external income
findings.detail: Placements are overspending by £8.8m, of which £1m comprises unachieved 2024-25 savings that were linked to additional grant or external income that did not materialise. Overspends span Independent and CWD Residential placements.
findings.matters: Placements are typically a council's largest and least controllable cost. Failed external income assumptions indicate the council is not securing anticipated grant funding, creating ongoing budget pressure.
findings.figures: £8.8m placements overspend; £1m unachieved BIP from 2024-25
findings.quote: £8.8m Placements pressure – includes £1m unachieved BIP and overspends in Independent and CWD Residential

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: Corporate contingencies of £22.8m released to balance budget, including £9.8m from 2024-25 Collection Fund surplus reserves
findings.detail: The council is drawing down £22.8m in corporate contingencies to fund in-year pressures, including £7.9m for homelessness and £5.1m for high-cost placements. Critically, £9.8m is reallocated from the previous year's Collection Fund surplus held in reserves, funding recurrent spending from one-off sources.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund current operations signals the council cannot balance ongoing revenue and ongoing spending. This erodes financial resilience and is unsustainable if spending pressures persist.
findings.figures: £22.8m contingencies released; £9.8m from Collection Fund surplus reserves
findings.quote: £22.8m corporate contingencies released: £7.9m for Homelessness §5.1m for high-cost placements §9.8m 2024-25 Collection Fund surplus reallocated from reserves to support the in year financial position

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy loss on Supported Exempt Accommodation overrunning by £3m largely due to government legislation
findings.detail: Housing & Support Services is experiencing a £3m overspend on Housing Benefit subsidy loss. The council attributes this primarily to government legislation, indicating this is a structural cost driver outside its direct control that will recur.
findings.matters: This represents recurring costs the council cannot unilaterally reduce. Lenders need visibility of how much budget pressure is legislative or demand-driven versus controllable through efficiency.
findings.figures: £3m overspend
findings.quote: Housing Benefit (HB) subsidy loss on Supported Exempt Accommodation set to overspend by £3m largely due to government legislation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: Planned DSG in-year overcommitment of £11.7m with Deficit Management Plan in development
findings.detail: SEN placement budgets are £3.2m over driven by delayed Health payments and increased demand at Freeman College. Additional pressures include Out of City Placements (£0.2m), EHCP top-ups (£0.7m), Post-16 provision (£1.5m), and Growth Fund (£3m). The council has built a £11.7m planned DSG overcommitment into its forecast.
findings.matters: DSG deficits create cumulative liability and must be recovered through future budget allocations. Rising SEND costs indicate demand growth that the council cannot absorb, a structural risk across English councils.
findings.figures: £11.7m planned DSG overcommitment; £3.2m SEN budget overspend
findings.quote: there is a planned in-year DSG overcommitment of £11.7m. A Deficit Management Plan is in development.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – 2025-26 Q2 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring v2
findings.headline: Adults Services delivered only £9.8m of £17.1m savings target (57% delivery rate), contributing to £29.5m overspend
findings.detail: Adults & Commissioning achieved less than 60% of planned savings, leaving a £9.8m shortfall. Additionally, £2.9m of remaining savings are marked undeliverable this year due to health budget constraints and limited income generation opportunities, suggesting structural dependency on external funding streams.
findings.matters: A 43% shortfall in the council's largest expense area signals that planned reductions cannot be reliably achieved. This creates ongoing budget pressure and indicates either poor planning capability or service-level factors that constrain savings delivery.
findings.figures: £9.8m delivered of £17.1m target; £2.9m undeliverable
findings.quote: Only £9.8m of £17.1m savings target delivered

news_drafts.headline: Transformation programme Future Sheffield delivering minimal financial benefit in 2025/26; majority of benefits deferred to future years
news_drafts.lead: If the council's medium-term financial strategy depends on transformation programme benefits that are not yet delivering, future budget years could face the same pressures as 2025/26 if the programme slips or underperforms.
news_drafts.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee

news_drafts.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) pressures in high needs continuing outside General Fund but remain material financial risk
news_drafts.lead: DSG deficits can accumulate as statutory duties that councils cannot avoid. Though accounted separately, high needs spending often spills into General Fund eventually, creating hidden future liabilities.
news_drafts.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee

news_drafts.headline: Housing structural deficit: £2.9m subsidy gap between cost and Housing Benefit recovery
news_drafts.lead: This is a structural mismatch between costs and income that cannot be solved by the council alone; it depends on government subsidy rules and the accuracy of provider claims. It is not a discretionary overspend but a policy-driven deficit.
news_drafts.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
